meta.title: Who really said "A culture of discipline is not a principle of business, it is a principle of greatness"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Verified: Jim Collins wrote it in his 2005 monograph Good to Great and the Social Sectors, as his reply to a CEO. The original uses a semicolon.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A culture of discipline is not a principle of business, it is a principle of greatness'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Jim Collins: from his November 2005 monograph Good to Great and the Social Sectors, his reply to a CEO who called discipline a business idea.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: b. 1958 · American business researcher and author
answer.sourceLine: Confirmed in Collins’s monograph Good to Great and the Social Sectors: Why Business Thinking Is Not the Answer (November 2005). There he remembers giving this answer to a CEO who argued that nonprofits needed “business” discipline. The original has a semicolon where the popular version has a comma.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Good to Great and the Social Sectors: Why Business Thinking Is Not the Answer

source.excerpt: “What makes you think that’s a business concept?” I replied. “Most businesses also have a desperate need for greater discipline. Mediocre companies rarely display the relentless culture of discipline—disciplined people who engage in disciplined thought and who take disciplined action—that we find in truly great companies. A culture of discipline is not a principle of business; it is a principle of greatness.”

source.excerptNote: Collins is replying to David Weekley, a CEO who had challenged him at a gathering of business leaders by saying nonprofits were “in desperate need of greater discipline.” The original uses a semicolon. Most quote sites print it with a comma.

author.bio: James C. “Jim” Collins is an American researcher and author who writes about what makes organizations last and grow. He is best known for Built to Last (1994, with Jerry I. Porras) and Good to Great (2001). In 2005 he followed up with a short monograph, Good to Great and the Social Sectors, that applies the same framework to nonprofits, schools, hospitals and government.

misattribution.heading: What gets mixed up
misattribution.intro: The credit to Collins is correct. What drifts as the line travels is its exact wording and where it came from.

items.why: Most quote sites print “…principle of business, it is a principle of greatness.” Collins’s text has a semicolon: “…principle of business; it is a principle of greatness” (jimcollins.com ↗). The words are the same. Only the punctuation changed.

items.who: “Discipline is not a business idea; it is a greatness idea”
items.why: This shorter version is a real Collins line too. It comes from a separate interview dated February 1, 2006, not from the monograph (Bridgespan ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Jim Collins wrote it in Good to Great and the Social Sectors (November 2005), as his own reply to a CEO’s challenge (excerpt ↗).

context.heading: Why he said it
lead: The monograph begins by rejecting the idea that the main path to greatness for nonprofits, schools and other social-sector groups is to become “more like a business.” Collins argues that most businesses are only mediocre or good, so copying business habits in general can mean copying mediocrity.

When he made that case to a room of business CEOs, David Weekley pushed back: nonprofits needed “greater discipline.” Collins’s reply was this line. Discipline, he said, is not something business owns. It is what separates great organizations from good ones in any sector.
